Regarding the "Counteracting of Erroneous Attachments": All erroneous attachments arise without exception based upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); if one is free from the view of self, there will be no erroneous attachments.
There are two kinds of views of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*): first, the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman-dṛṣṭi*), and second, the view of a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātman-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the view of a personal self, five types are taught based on the common worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*):

First, as stated in the sūtras, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is ultimately quiescent, like empty space. When the foolish and ignorant hear this, they fail to understand its meaning and instead cling to the notion that the nature of the Tathāgata is identical to empty space—eternal, constant, and omnipresent.

To eliminate that attachment, it is clarified that the characteristic of space is merely a conceptual construction and is ultimately unattainable; when there is seeing and opposition toward various forms, the mind conceptually designates it by the name "space."

Since form is merely the conceptual construction of the deluded mind, one should know that space likewise has no substantial essence; all objective phenomena are nothing other than the conceptual constructions of the deluded mind.
If one is free from the deluded mind, then the appearances of objective realms cease; there is only the Tathatā-mind, which is all-pervasive.
This is the meaning of the Tathagata’s self-nature being like space; it does not mean that like space, it is permanent or existent.
Second, as it is said in the sutras: all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty, and even suchness and the dharmas of nirvana are ultimately empty; their original nature is thus devoid of all marks.
Ordinary, ignorant people, upon hearing this, do not understand its meaning and instead cling to the notion that the *dharmatā* of *nirvāṇa* and *tathatā* is merely empty and devoid of substance.

To eliminate such clinging, it is clarified that the essential nature of the *tathatā-dharmakāya* is not empty, for it is fully endowed with immeasurable qualities of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
Third, as stated in the sūtras, the tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with all essential qualities and virtues, neither increasing nor decreasing.

When ordinary, ignorant people hear this, they fail to understand its meaning and instead cling to the notion that the tathāgatagarbha possesses the distinct characteristics of material and mental phenomena.

To eliminate this attachment, it is clarified that while True Suchness (tathatā) is fundamentally free from the distinctions of defiled phenomena, it is established as possessing the characteristics of boundless virtues, rather than being characterized by defilement.
Fourth, as stated in the sūtras, all the various defiled phenomena of the world arise based upon the Tathāgatagarbha; all phenomena are not distinct from True Suchness.
When ordinary, ignorant people hear this, they do not understand its meaning and claim that the *tathāgatagarbha* possesses all the defiled phenomena of the world.

To eliminate this misconception, it is clarified that the *tathāgatagarbha* has, from the very beginning, possessed pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, which are non-different from *tathatā* (suchness); whereas the defiled phenomena of the afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges are merely falsely existent, lacking inherent nature (*svabhāva*) from the start, and have never for a moment been associated with the *tathāgatagarbha* since time immemorial.
If it were the case that the Tathāgatagarbha is associated with defiled dharmas such that one could realize and bring to rest these deluded defilements, this would be impossible.
Fifth, as stated in the sutras, based upon the Tathāgatagarbha there is saṃsāra and the attainment of nirvāṇa.

When ordinary, ignorant people hear this, they do not understand its meaning; they claim that based on the *tathāgatagarbha*, birth and death have a beginning, and because they perceive a beginning, they further claim that *nirvāṇa* has an end.
To eliminate this attachment, it is clarified that the Tathāgatagarbha has no beginning; based upon it, the cycle of birth and death through ignorance is beginningless.
If one were to say that there are sentient beings who first arise outside the triple world, such is what is taught in the scriptures of non-Buddhists, not the Buddha's teaching.
Because the Tathāgatagarbha has no posterior limit, one realizes the eternal severance of the seeds of birth and death, thereby attaining Nirvāṇa which likewise has no posterior limit.
Based on the view of a personal self (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), four kinds of views arise; therefore, those four are established upon this basis.
Regarding the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātmadṛṣṭi*): because the two vehicles possess dull faculties, the World-Honored One taught them only the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
Those individuals then become ultimately attached to the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates; they fear birth and death and falsely grasp at nirvāṇa.

To eliminate this attachment, it is clarified that the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates is non-arising; because they do not arise, they also have no cessation; and because they do not cease, they are primordially nirvāṇa.
If one is ultimately free from discriminative attachment, one will know that all defiled and pure phenomena are established only in mutual dependence.

Therefore, one should understand that all dharmas, from the very beginning, are neither form nor mind, neither wisdom nor consciousness, neither non-existent nor existent; they are, in the final analysis, entirely of an ineffable nature.

Any verbal expressions used for instruction and teaching are all the Tathāgata’s skillful means; he provisionally employs language to guide sentient beings, enabling them to abandon words and enter into reality.
If one clings to the meaning according to the words, false discrimination will increase, true wisdom will not arise, and nirvana will not be attained.

To discriminate the characteristics of practicing the right path means that it is the primary cause for all Tathāgatas to attain the Way, and because all Bodhisattvas resolve their minds to cultivate it so that it may manifest before them.

Briefly stated, there are three aspects of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*): first, the generation of the mind through the perfection of faith; second, the generation of the mind through the stage of practice based on understanding; and third, the generation of the mind through realization. Regarding the generation of the mind through the perfection of faith:
in what stage does it rely, and by practicing what conduct is one able to achieve the perfection of faith and become capable of generating the mind?

It should be known that such a person relies on the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi); through the power of roots of goodness perfumed by the Dharma, they develop deep faith in the retribution of karma and practice the ten paths of wholesome action. Disgusted with the suffering of birth and death, they seek supreme enlightenment; encountering various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they serve and make offerings to them while practicing all manner of deeds. Only after ten thousand kalpas does their faith reach fulfillment.

From this point onward, they may resolve their minds [on awakening] through the power of the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or through great compassion, or because the True Dharma is about to perish; it is for the sake of protecting the Dharma that they are able to generate the aspiration.

Once they have resolved their minds, they enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and never again regress, abiding in the superior cause that corresponds to the Buddha-lineage (*buddha-gotra*).

There may be sentient beings who, from time immemorial, have had meager roots of goodness; because their afflictions (*kleśa*) are so profound that they shroud their minds, even though they encounter various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and serve and make offerings to them, they plant only the seeds for rebirth as humans or devas, or plant the seeds for the enlightenment of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). Or there may be those who, though seeking the path to great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), are of indeterminate faculties, sometimes advancing and sometimes retreating. Or there may be those who encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, making offerings and serving them while practicing various deeds, yet fail to fulfill [their practice] within ten thousand great eons, instead encountering conditions along the way to resolve their minds [for enlightenment].
By what conditions does this occur?

It refers to either seeing the physical form of a Buddha, making offerings to the Sangha, being instructed by those of the two vehicles, or witnessing others resolve their minds [for enlightenment]. These instances of generating the mind are all yet undetermined; if one encounters adverse conditions, one may at times fall back and descend to the level of the two vehicles.

Furthermore, the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith is briefly explained as being threefold: first, the arousal of an upright mind, because one maintains correct mindfulness of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) according to reality;
second, the arousal of a profound and earnest mind, because one delights in accumulating all virtuous practices;
and third, the arousal of a mind of great compassion, because one vows to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.
Question:

Since all sentient beings and all phenomena are of one and the same dharma-realm and possess no dual characteristics, according to principle one should simply maintain right mindfulness of True Suchness (tathatā). Why, then, is it necessary to further cultivate all manner of wholesome practices to save all sentient beings?
Answer: It is not so.

For example, a mani jewel is by its very nature bright and pure; yet if it remains amidst impurities and dross, even if someone were to apply diligent mindfulness toward it, they would never be able to obtain its purity if they did not employ skillful means or exert effort.

The Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is likewise: although its essence is luminous and pure, fully endowed with all merits, it is defiled by boundless adventitious dust. Even if someone were to apply diligent mindfulness, yet fail to employ skillful means or cultivate various practices, there is no principle by which they could ever attain purity.
Therefore, one must certainly gather all wholesome practices and rescue all sentient beings, thereby departing from those boundless adventitious defilements and manifesting the True Dharma.
Those expedient practices are briefly of four kinds:
first, the fundamental expedient practice.
This refers to contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unborn, thereby departing from false views and not abiding in birth and death.

Furthermore, observing that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and that the fruits of karma are never lost, they give rise to great compassion and cultivate various wholesome deeds, gathering and transforming sentient beings while not dwelling in nirvana.

Because True Suchness is free from the characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, this practice is taken as the fundamental basis of conformity; this is called the skillful means of the fundamental basis of practice.
Second is the skillful means of cessation.
That which is called shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and repentance (*deśanā*) can cause all unwholesome dharmas to cease and not increase.
Because *tathatā* is free from all characteristics of fault, one accords with *tathatā* to bring all evils to rest; this is called the skillful means for cessation.
Third is the skillful means for growing roots of goodness:

that is, to give rise to a heart of love and reverence toward the Triple Gem, honoring, making offerings to, prostrating before, and praising them; to rejoice in their merits, to entreat them [for teachings], and to increase one’s right faith, even to the point of aspiring for unsurpassed bodhi. Thus protected by the majestic power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one’s karmic obstacles are purified and one’s roots of goodness do not regress.

Because True Suchness is free from all obstacles and endowed with all meritorious qualities, practicing wholesome deeds in accordance with True Suchness is called the skillful means for cultivating and growing roots of goodness.
The four great vows are the skillful means of equality.
This refers to making a vow to reach the end of the future, to equally rescue and deliver all sentient beings, and to cause them to abide securely in nirvana without remainder.

Because they know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-dual, because they are equal in this and that, and because they are ultimately quiescent, they give rise to great vows in accordance with these three aspects of suchness; this is called the skillful means of the equality of the great vow.

When a bodhisattva thus arouses the mind, they obtain a partial vision of the Buddha’s Dharma-body and are able to manifest eight types of deeds according to their power of aspiration: namely, descending from the Tuṣita heaven, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving home, attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.
Nevertheless, they are not yet called the Dharmakāya because the out-flowing (sāsrava) karma from immeasurable past eons has not been eliminated.
Due to this evil karma, they may experience slight suffering; however, sustained by the power of their vows, they are not bound for long.

In certain sūtras it is said that bodhisattvas who have brought forth the mind through the perfection of faith may sometimes fall back into the evil destinies; this refers to beginners whose minds are largely characterized by indolence and who have not yet entered the stage of certainty. These words were spoken to increase their vigor and resolve, and are not a statement of ultimate reality.

Furthermore, once this bodhisattva has generated the mind of enlightenment, they cultivate various ascetic practices for their own benefit and the benefit of others with a mind free from cowardice; they do not even fear falling into the stages of the two vehicles, much less into the evil realms.

If one hears that it is only after diligently practicing various difficult and painful austerities for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas that one finally attains Buddhahood, one feels neither alarm nor fear; how much less would one give rise to the mind of the two vehicles or fall into the evil destinies? This is because one possesses the resolute conviction that all dharmas have been in the nature of nirvāṇa from the very beginning.

One should know that the generation of the mind through the stage of practice and understanding is increasingly superior, because the first incalculable eon is about to be completed, because one has attained profound understanding within True Suchness (tathatā), and because one cultivates all practices without attachment.

This Bodhisattva knows that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from the characteristics of stinginess and greed; this is the pure perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), and he practices the perfection of giving in accordance with it.

He knows that the nature of phenomena is free from the objects of the five desires and devoid of the characteristics of breaking precepts; this is the pure perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), and he practices the perfection of ethical discipline in accordance with it.

He knows that the nature of phenomena is without suffering and affliction and free from the characteristics of anger and harm; this is the pure perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), and he practices the perfection of patience in accordance with it.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is free from the characteristics of body and mind and is without indolence is the pure perfection of vigor; one accordingly practices the *vīryapāramitā*.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is unmoving and undisturbed is the pure perfection of meditation; one accordingly practices the *dhyānapāramitā*.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is free from all darkness of delusion is the pure perfection of wisdom; one accordingly practices the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the realization of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), this extends from the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*) up to the Ultimate Stage of the Bodhisattva (*bodhisattvanisthābhūmi*).
What is the realm realized?
It is called "suchness" (*tathatā*) when described as a realm in reliance upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*); however, in actual realization, there is no appearance of a realm.

Because this Bodhisattva, by means of non-conceptual wisdom, realizes the dharmakāya of true suchness that transcends verbal expression, he is able, in a single thought-moment, to travel throughout all worlds in the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas and request them to turn the wheel of Dharma. He acts solely for the benefit of sentient beings and does not seek to hear or receive beautiful words and phrases.
Alternatively, for the sake of those sentient beings who are timid and weak, he manifests great diligence to transcend immeasurable kalpas and swiftly attain perfect enlightenment;
or, for the sake of those sentient beings who are indolent, he passes through immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, practicing asceticism for a long time before finally attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, he manifests countless skillful means, all for the benefit of all sentient beings.

Yet, in reality, the spiritual lineage, faculties, initial resolve, and realization of all bodhisattvas are entirely equal; there is no dharma by which one may surpass another, for it is certain that they all attain perfect enlightenment after passing through three incalculable eons.
However, according to the differences among the worlds of sentient beings—and because their perceptions, faculties, desires, and natures vary—they are shown various distinctions in their practices.
This realization within the arising of the mind consists of three types of mind:
first, the true mind, because it is free from discrimination;
Second is the mind of skillful means, because it spontaneously benefits others;
third is the mind of karmic consciousness, because its arising and ceasing are subtle.

Furthermore, once this Bodhisattva has perfected both types of adornment—merit and wisdom—he attains a body most supreme among all worlds in the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, he suddenly uproots the root of ignorance and becomes endowed with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Possessing inconceivable activity that occurs spontaneously, he universally transforms sentient beings throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
Question:

Because space is infinite, the worlds are infinite; because the worlds are infinite, sentient beings are infinite; and because sentient beings are infinite, the distinctions in their mental activities are likewise infinite.
Such objects of experience are without limit and are difficult to know and difficult to comprehend.
If ignorance were severed such that mental characteristics were forever absent, how could one be able to understand all aspects and achieve the knowledge of all aspects?
Answer:

All delusive objects have, from the very beginning, in reality, the single mind as their sole nature. Yet all sentient beings, by clinging to these delusive objects, are unable to know the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of all phenomena.

The Buddhas and Tathāgatas, being free from all clinging, are able to directly perceive the true nature of all phenomena; they possess great wisdom that illuminates the distinctions between all defiled and pure states, and through immeasurable and boundless skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings according to their needs.
Therefore, when the deluded mind is extinguished, one comprehends all aspects and accomplishes the knowledge of all aspects.
Question:

If all Buddhas possess boundless skillful means and are able to spontaneously benefit all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, why is it that sentient beings do not constantly see the Buddha, nor witness his miraculous transformations, nor hear him preach the Dharma?
Answer:
The Tathāgata truly possesses such skillful means, yet he manifests his body only when waiting for the minds of sentient beings to become pure.
It is like a mirror: when there is grime, reflections do not appear; once the grime is removed, they appear.
Sentient beings are likewise: as long as the mind has not yet been freed from defilement, the Dharma-body does not manifest;
once freed from defilement, it manifests.
How, then, does one cultivate the factor of faith?
This is spoken with reference to sentient beings who have not yet entered the correct concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
What constitutes faith?
How is it to be cultivated?
There are four kinds of faith:
first, faith in the root, which means delighting in mindfulness of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma;

second, faith that the Buddha is endowed with boundless merit, which means constantly and joyfully prostrating, revering, making offerings, hearing the true Dharma, practicing according to the Dharma, and dedicating [the merit] toward omniscience.
Third, faith in the Dharma brings great benefit, because it leads one to constantly delight in practicing the various pāramitās.

Fourth, faith in the Sangha of right practice, because it leads one to constantly make offerings to the assembly of bodhisattvas and correctly cultivate practices for both self-benefit and the benefit of others.

Cultivating the practices of the five gates can bring this faith to fulfillment; namely, the gate of giving, the gate of precepts, the gate of patience, the gate of diligence, and the gate of tranquility and insight.
How does one cultivate the gate of giving?

That is to say, when seeing sentient beings come to beg from him, he bestows his own wealth and resources upon them according to his ability, relinquishing his own stinginess and attachment so that they may rejoice.
When seeing sentient beings oppressed by peril and distress, he employs skillful means to rescue and relieve them, ensuring they are free from fear.
If there are sentient beings who come to seek the Dharma, one should explain it according to what one understands and as is appropriate for them.

When practicing these three kinds of giving, one does not do so for the sake of fame, nor does one seek gain or offerings, nor is one greedily attached to worldly rewards; rather, one keeps in mind only the benefit and happiness of oneself and others, dedicating the merit toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What is the cultivation of the gate of ethical discipline?

It means that a lay bodhisattva should distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, avarice, anger, envy, flattery, deception, and wrong views.

If one has left the household life, for the sake of subduing all afflictions, one should distance oneself from clamor and always rely on tranquility; one should practice contentment and the dhūta austerities, and even regarding minor transgressions, give rise to great fear, shame, and remorse. One should uphold the prohibitive precepts established by the Tathāgata so as not to cause those who see them to harbor criticism or disdain, and should enable sentient beings to abandon evil and cultivate goodness.
What is the practice of the gate of patience? It is said:
not loathing others when seeing their faults, remaining unmoved when encountering suffering, and always delighting in contemplating the profound meaning of the words and phrases.
What is the practice of the gate of diligence?
This means that in practicing all virtuous deeds, one’s mind must not slacken or retreat.

One should reflect that throughout incalculable eons in the past, for the sake of seeking the objects of worldly desire, one has pointlessly endured all manner of great physical and mental suffering, yet ultimately there was not even a fraction of true flavor to be found.
To ensure that such suffering is abandoned in the future, one should exert diligent effort without giving rise to indolence, benefiting all sentient beings through great compassion.

Although a beginner bodhisattva practices with faith, because they have accumulated many grave sins and karmic obstructions over successive lifetimes, they may be afflicted by demons and heterodox influences, entangled by worldly affairs, or oppressed by various causes of illness. Such obstacles are manifold, causing the practitioner to abandon the cultivation of wholesome qualities.

Therefore, you should practice with courageous diligence, worshipping the Buddhas during the six periods of day and night, making offerings, praising them, repenting, requesting [the turning of the wheel of Dharma], rejoicing in merit, and dedicating [the roots of goodness] toward unexcelled Bodhi. You should make great vows without ceasing, so that evil obstructions are eliminated and roots of goodness increase.
What is the method for cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā?

The cessation of all conceptual proliferation regarding objects is the meaning of śamatha; clearly perceiving the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of cause and effect is the meaning of vipaśyanā.
Initially, one practices each separately; as they gradually increase, one reaches the stage of spontaneous dual cultivation upon attainment.

Regarding the practice of *śamatha*: dwelling in a quiet place, sit cross-legged with the body upright and the mind rectified. Do not rely on the breath, do not rely on forms or colors, do not rely on space, and do not rely on earth, water, fire, or wind, even to the point of not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Eliminate all discursive thoughts and mental conceptions, and even eliminate the thought of elimination itself, because all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing and are entirely without marks.

The preceding mind relies upon an object and subsequently relinquishes that object; the succeeding thought relies upon the mind and further relinquishes that mind. This is because the mind was previously distracted by external objects and had to be gathered and stabilized within; subsequently, one again gives rise to a mind that does not grasp at the characteristics of the mind itself, for apart from True Suchness (tathatā), nothing can be apprehended.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, at all times one should practice in this manner without interruption; thus, one will gradually enter the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā), ultimately subduing all afflictions, increasing in faith, and swiftly attaining the stage of non-retrogression.
Those who harbor doubts and slander with lack of faith, those shrouded by karmic obstructions, and those possessed of pride and indolence—such persons are unable to enter it.

Furthermore, by relying on this samādhi, one realizes the characteristics of the dharma-realm, knowing that the dharma-body of all Tathāgatas and the bodies of all sentient beings are equal and non-dual, being of a single characteristic; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic.
If one cultivates this samādhi, one can give rise to immeasurable samādhis, because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the fundamental basis of all samādhis.

There may be sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight, who are deluded and distracted by various Māras, non-Buddhists, and spirits; these may manifest evil forms to terrify their minds, or display beautiful colors to bewilder their intentions. They may manifest the forms of devas, bodhisattvas, or even Buddhas adorned with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), or they may preach *dhāraṇīs*, or preach the various perfections (*pāramitās*). Or again, they may expound upon the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), saying that there is no enemy and no friend, no cause and no fruit, and that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, being by nature in *nirvāṇa*.
Or again, they may cause them to know the events of the past, future, and the minds of others, expounding with eloquence and without impediment.
They sever [their progress] by causing them to become attached to fame and gain; or by being frequently angry or frequently joyful;
or by having excessive sorrow or excessive affection; or by constantly delighting in drowsiness and sleep, or by not sleeping for long periods;
or by being afflicted with physical illness; or by being by nature indolent and lacking in exertion; or by suddenly initiating vigor only to abandon it immediately; or by having many worldly desires.

Doubt arises such that they do not develop faith or acceptance; or they abandon their original superior practices to cultivate miscellaneous karmas, becoming attached to worldly affairs and drowning in their passions for what is pleasant;

or they cause them to attain various meditative concentrations of external paths, remaining in those concentrations for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, obtaining fine food and drink, with body and mind feeling at ease, neither hungry nor thirsty.
Alternatively, they may be exhorted to accept female forms and the like; or their food and drink may be made to fluctuate between scarcity and abundance;
or their physical appearance may be rendered beautiful or ugly. If they are thus disturbed by various views and afflictions, they will immediately fall away from their former roots of goodness.
Therefore, one should carefully and thoroughly examine this and form this thought:
"All of this is because my roots of goodness are feeble and my karmic obstructions are heavy, causing me to be deluded by demons, ghosts, and the like."
Having understood this, one contemplates that all these are merely mind.
Through such reflection, thoughts perish in each instant; remaining free from all signs, one enters true samādhi.

Once the characteristics of the mind have departed, the true nature is also exhausted; upon arising from meditative concentration, all views and afflictions no longer manifest, because their seeds have been destroyed by the power of samādhi.
Excellently virtuous qualities will follow in succession, all obstacles and difficulties will be entirely removed, and one will give rise to great diligence that is constant and uninterrupted.
If one does not practice this samādhi, there is no way to enter the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Because all other samādhis possess signs and are shared with non-Buddhists, one cannot encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through them.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should diligently practice this samādhi to bring it to ultimate perfection.
By practicing this samādhi, one’s present body immediately attains ten kinds of benefits:
first, one is constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions;
second, one is not troubled or disturbed by any demons or malevolent spirits.
Third, they will not be deluded by any heterodox paths;
fourth, the karmic obstructions resulting from the grave offense of slandering the profound Dharma will all be rendered thin and light;
fifth, all doubts and various evil discursive thoughts will be extinguished.
Sixth, one’s faith in the realm of the Tathāgata increases;
seventh, being free from sorrow and regret, one is courageous and undaunted amidst birth and death;
eighth, being free from arrogance, gentle, and patient, one is constantly revered by all the world.
Ninth, even if one does not abide in meditative concentration, the seeds of affliction within all times and all objects are so attenuated that they never manifest;
tenth, if one abides in meditative concentration, one is not disturbed or distracted by any conditions such as sounds and the like.

Furthermore, if one practices only śamatha, the mind will become sunken or give rise to indolence; one will not delight in various virtues and will distance oneself from great compassion. Therefore, one should practice vipaśyanā concurrently.
How should one practice?

It means that one should contemplate how all phenomena in the world arise and perish without ceasing; because they are impermanent, they are suffering; and because they are suffering, they are non-self.
One should contemplate past phenomena as like a dream, present phenomena as like lightning, and future phenomena as like clouds that arise suddenly.
One should contemplate that this body is entirely impure, a mixture of various worms, filth, and afflictions.
One observes that the phenomena perceived by ordinary, ignorant people are falsely conceived as existing within a state of non-existence.
One examines all phenomena arising from conditions and sees that they are like illusions and the like, ultimately devoid of reality.
One contemplates that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is not within the sphere of the mind; it cannot be illustrated by analogy and cannot be expressed in words.

One observes all sentient beings who, from time immemorial, have experienced immeasurable physical and mental suffering due to the power of the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*). This remains the case for the present and the future as well; they are boundless and limitless, difficult to escape and difficult to liberate. Constantly dwelling therein, they fail to realize their condition, which is truly to be pitied.

Having contemplated thus, one gives rise to definitive wisdom, engenders vast compassion, arouses great valor, and establishes a great vow: "May my mind be freed from all perversions and sever all conceptual discriminations; may I draw near to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, prostrating, making offerings, revering, and praising them; may I hear the True Dharma and practice according to its teachings, without ceasing until the end of the future."
By means of immeasurable skillful means, one rescues all sentient beings from the ocean of suffering and establishes them in the ultimate bliss of nirvāṇa.

Having made this vow, at all times and according to one's capacity, one practices the conduct that benefits both oneself and others; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one constantly and diligently observes what should and should not be done—this is called the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, if one practices only insight (vipaśyanā), the mind will not come to rest; it will give rise to much doubt and fail to accord with the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), nor will the non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) arise. Therefore, calm abiding (śamatha) and insight should be practiced together.

This means that although one contemplates that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvana, one nevertheless perceives that the retribution for good and evil karma resulting from the conjunction of causes and conditions is neither lost nor destroyed.

Although one contemplates the causes and conditions of the retribution for good and evil karma, one simultaneously perceives that all phenomena are without arising, without intrinsic nature, and even [identical to] nirvana.

Nevertheless, the practice of *śamatha* serves as an antidote to the ordinary person’s attachment to birth and death, and it also remedies the fear born from the two vehicles’ clinging to birth and death.

For those who practice contemplation, it serves as an antidote to ordinary beings' failure to cultivate roots of goodness, and it also remedies the fault of the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their narrow, inferior minds.
Therefore, calm abiding and insight mutually support and perfect one another, never being separated.
If one lacks both tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), one will certainly be unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, when a beginner bodhisattva dwells in this Sahā world, they may encounter the sufferings of cold, heat, wind, rain, untimely seasons, famine, and so forth; or they may see sentient beings who are unwholesome and terrifying, entangled by the three poisons, possessed of inverted wrong views, and who abandon the path of goodness to practice evil dharmas.

If a bodhisattva, while in the midst of practice, gives rise to timidity and weakness, fearing that they may not encounter the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, or fearing that they cannot achieve pure faith, and thus develops doubt and wishes to retreat, they should reflect as follows:

"All the Buddhas and bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions have attained great supernormal powers without obstruction, and are able to rescue and deliver all sentient beings in perilous distress through various skillful means."
Having formed this thought, they make a great vow and single-mindedly focus their mindfulness on the Buddha and the bodhisattvas.

Because they have given rise to such a resolute mind, at the end of this life they will certainly attain rebirth in another buddha-field, where they shall behold the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, perfect their faith, and forever leave behind the evil realms.
As it is said in the sutra:

"If a son or daughter of good family single-mindedly recollects Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates all roots of goodness with the vow to be born there, they will certainly attain birth."
Constantly beholding that Buddha, their faith increases and they never again fall back.
Hearing the Dharma from him and contemplating the Buddha’s Dharma-body, they gradually practice and attain entry into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
What is the section on benefits?
Thus, the secret meaning of these Mahāyāna phrases has now been briefly explained.

If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to a mind of pure faith, awakening, and understanding regarding the vast Dharma within the profound realm of the Tathāgata, and who desire to enter the path of the Mahāyāna without obstruction, they should diligently listen to, receive, contemplate, and practice this brief treatise. It should be known that such persons will certainly and swiftly accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If one hears this Dharma and does not give rise to fear or alarm, it should be known that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and will swiftly receive a prophecy of enlightenment.

Suppose there were someone who transformed all sentient beings in the three thousandfold world system, causing them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action; this would not equal even a moment’s correct contemplation of this Dharma, for its merit would surpass the former by an immeasurable and boundless degree.
If one practices as taught for even a single day and night, the merit produced will be immeasurable, boundless, and beyond description.

Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to speak for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they could not exhaust it; for since the merit of *tathatā* (suchness) is without limit, the merit of practice is likewise without limit.
If one gives rise to slander toward this Dharma, one incurs immeasurable sin and will undergo great suffering for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Therefore, one should maintain firm faith in it and not give rise to slander; to do so would be to harm oneself and others, and to sever the seeds of the Triple Gem.
All Buddhas have relied upon this practice to achieve unsurpassed wisdom; all Bodhisattvas have realized the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body by means of this.

Past Bodhisattvas relied upon it to attain great Mahāyāna pure faith; those of the present are now attaining it, and those of the future shall attain it. Therefore, those who wish to become practitioners of the sublime path that benefits both self and others should diligently study and cultivate this treatise.
I have now explained the profound and vast meaning;
may its merit be bestowed upon all sentient beings, enabling them to perceive the Dharma of True Suchness.
*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Fascicle II.
